segments.description: Coaches, I welcome Wayne Elderton to our conference, one of Canada's most respected coach educators and a national expert on game-based coaching. Wayne has created much of the Canadian certification curriculum and has been recognised with numerous coaching awards. In his presentation, situational play, Wayne takes a deep dive in how to structure your sessions to be more representative of the game. Please welcome Wayne as he shares his expertise in this subject. Wayne, welcome. Hello, my name is Wayne Elderton and I'm a tennis Canada coach developer, certified at the coach for and club professional three levels, a PTR international master professional and the tennis director of the North Vancouver Tennis Centre. We're going to look at a concept called situational point play. This fits into an overall approach that I call situation training, which is a variation of the game-based approach. Situation training is based on the premise that tennis uses open skills. Open skills require perception, problem solving and decision making before applying technique. In an open skill, technique is how a player solves tactical problems they encounter during play. Global technique in tennis is less about perfecting the perfect form as it is about adaptation. To empower players to learn the open skill of tennis, the goal of situation training is about expanding the library of situations players can handle at their level of play

through effective and efficient technique and to build a foundation for success at future levels. Something that focuses on isolated stroke technique disconnected to the situations it occurs doesn't fully equip players for the reality of tennis. Situation training uses a specific session structure. It starts with athletic development and moves into fundamental volume training. Now if anyone is interested, there's a video on acecoachcoach.com on my YouTube channel about fundamental volume training. But then it continues with the main body of the session being a section on tactical and technical training. The tactical and technical training section splits into three parts that follow a play-practice-play format. The point-play components of play-practice-play are what I call situational point-play and that is what we're going to look at in more detail in just a moment. The first situational point-play is to gain exposure to the situation and foreclosures to see what the players actually do in the situation. Then the skills needed to be successful in the situation are trained in a practice piece and finally the session ends with situational point-play but it's geared to integrate the skills learned in the practice into their play. Most coaches will incorporate some kind of point-play in sessions. Typically it'll be playing points at the end of a session. Now this is a good thing but the point-play at that end of the session is usually disconnected.

What's more powerful is to connect the point-play to what was practiced in the session. The classic example would be a session where players were training overheads at the net. No matter how many points are played at the end of the session, only a couple of overheads if any may happen at all. Coaches need a systematic way to ensure that the situation trained in the session is occurring in the point-play so players can understand the tactics of the skills used and integrate the technical skills that they learned. In other words, the point-play needs to be directly connected to the situation being practiced. This is where situational point-play comes in. The structure of connected situational point-play begins with identifying five general situations that occur as a stereotypical point unfolds. Imagine a point being played. It begins with a serve and then a return. Next is a baseline exchange where the players are both back. A player then could get a shortball and approach the net and they come in to volley or hit overheads. Then the player could respond with passing shots. Of course, all these situations might not happen in every point. For example, a serve and a volley may bypass the both-back exchange. These are just all the possible general situations that could occur during a point. Situational point-play will use these five categories to create point-play games based on the five point situations.

To practically apply the five point situations, I've created a fun little motto to remind coaches how they can modify the point-play. The motto reads, you can start a point, at any point, in the point. This is helpful so a coach knows that point-play doesn't have to start with a serve and only use full points. Earlier we imagined that stereotypical point, with all the five point situations unfolding. A coach can actually parachute into any of the five point-play situations, imagining that the others have already occurred. For example, if the focus in our practice is the approach in that net situation, we can modify our point-play by imagining there was already a serve, already a return, and a baseline exchange already happened that produced a shortball. And here is where we'll actually start the situational point-play. So you can start a point, at any point, in the point. If we zoom into the five point situations, we can focus on the specific situation of a specific shot, which we call in our system the shot cycle. That looks a little complex, but I'll just go over it a bit. In our Canadian system, we don't actually talk about strokes, like forehands and backhands and serves and volleys as much as we deal with what we call shots. Each shot, or shot cycle, has two halves. The first is everything a player must deal with to receive the ball. This creates the situation and presents a problem for the player to solve.

It includes the ball received, the location of the players, and the perception or the anticipation that can occur. The second half is the response to the situation. This is where the player solves the problem by responding with their projection of the ball. It includes which stroke they use, but also the characteristics of the ball sent and the phase of play, in other words, if the shot is neutral or offense or defense. Finally, there's a recovery before the entire cycle repeats again for the next shot. During any situational point play, the coach should refrain from jumping in and coaching, but rather they need to observe, take some mental notes on how successful the players are at that situation and where they need the work, let the players experience the situation, just be a cheerleader and a play organizer during situational point play. In summary, in a situational training session during the tactical technical training portion of the session, we actually use, again, a play practice play format. We connect playing points to what is being trained by making the point play distinctly situational point play. We do this by using two coaching tools. The five point situations tool gives us a general framework to define situations. This tool comes with the motto, again, you can start a point at any point in the point, so we can get sufficient repetition for the situation. The shot cycle tool allows us to define the specific situation to deal with. It informs the coach of the unique elements of that situation, that they need to recreate with all of its distinctiveness. And finally, after the situational point play, the coaches should present their findings and inspire the players to practice the shots needed to be successful in the situation.
